chunks: "A resistor, specifically a variable series resistor.
The pass transistor sits between the input and the load and drops the excess voltage, so at any operating point it looks like a resistor of R equals (V in-V out) over I out .

The feedback loop continuously changes that resistance to hold the output constant: if the load draws more current, the loop lowers the resistance so the drop stays the same size relative to what's needed, and if the input rises, it increases the resistance.
That model gives me the key facts straight away.
The power lost is I to the 2R , which is (V in-V out) times I out , so it's the same heat as a fixed dropper resistor, but the output doesn't sag with load.
The efficiency is V out over V in since the same current flows in and out.
And at dropout the loop has run out of range, so the resistor is at its minimum, R DS(on) , and the output is just V in-I R DS(on) .

If someone wants the small-signal picture, the closed-loop output impedance is very low at DC and rises with frequency like an inductor until the loop runs out of gain, which is why the output capacitor takes over."
